items.stem: When a polythene rod is rubbed with a cloth it becomes negatively charged. Why?
options: Electrons move from the cloth to the rod
Positive charges are created in the cloth
Electrons move from the rod to the cloth
Protons move from the rod to the cloth
items.answer: Electrons move from the cloth to the rod
items.markingKey: Only electrons move in charging by friction; the rod gains electrons.

items.stem: A rubbed balloon sticks to a neutral wall. Explain why.
items.answer: The negative balloon repels electrons in the wall surface away, leaving the surface positively charged by induction; unlike charges attract.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: charge induced in wall; 1 mark: attraction of unlike charges.

items.stem: Explain why a metal rod held in the hand cannot be charged by rubbing, but a plastic rod can.
items.answer: Metal is a conductor, so any charge flows away through the hand to earth; plastic is an insulator so charge stays where it is.

items.stem: A rod gains a charge of −1.6 × 10⁻⁹ C when rubbed. The charge on one electron is −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Calculate how many electrons were transferred to the rod.
items.answer: 1.0 × 10¹⁰ electrons

items.stem: A rod gains a charge of −8.0 × 10⁻⁹ C when rubbed. The charge on one electron is −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Calculate how many electrons were transferred to the rod.
items.answer: 5.0 × 10¹⁰ electrons

items.stem: A acetate strip is rubbed with a cotton cloth and becomes positively charged with a charge of magnitude 3.2 × 10⁻⁹ C. (a) Explain, in terms of electrons, how the rod became charged. (b) Explain why the same experiment does not work with a metal rod held in the hand.
items.answer: (a) Electrons moved off the acetate strip onto the cloth. (b) Charge flows through the conducting metal and the body to earth.

items.stem: Two negatively charged balloons are held close together. What happens?
items.answer: They repel each other

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which of these is a good electrical insulator? (b) When a polythene rod is rubbed with a cloth it becomes negatively charged. Why?
items.answer: (a) Plastic (b) Electrons move from the cloth to the rod
items.markingKey: (a) Insulators (plastic, rubber, glass, dry wood) do not let electrons move freely. (b) Only electrons move in charging by friction; the rod gains electrons.

items.stem: Explain why charging by friction cannot produce a positive charge by "adding protons".
items.answer: Protons are fixed in the nuclei; only electrons are free to move, so an object becomes positive by losing electrons.

items.stem: A student rubs a glass rod with silk and it becomes positive. Explain what has happened to the silk and why.
items.answer: The silk gains the electrons lost by the glass, so it becomes equally negatively charged; charge is conserved.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: silk negative; 1 mark: equal and opposite (conservation).

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why charging by friction cannot produce a positive charge by "adding protons". (b) A rubbed balloon sticks to a neutral wall. Explain why.
items.answer: (a) Protons are fixed in the nuclei; only electrons are free to move, so an object becomes positive by losing electrons. (b) The negative balloon repels electrons in the wall surface away, leaving the surface positively charged by induction; unlike charges attract.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each. (b) 1 mark: charge induced in wall; 1 mark: attraction of unlike charges.

items.stem: Two identical metal spheres on insulating stands carry charges of +8 nC and −4 nC. They touch briefly and are separated. Calculate the final charge on each and explain.
items.answer: 2.00 nC each: electrons move until charge is shared equally between identical spheres; total charge is conserved.
items.markingKey: 1 mark total; 1 mark shared equally; 1 mark conservation.

To stop charge building up and causing a spark that ignites fuel vapour
To make the fuel flow faster

items.stem: Explain how an electrostatic paint sprayer gives an even coat and wastes less paint.
items.answer: Paint droplets are given the same charge, so they repel and spread out; the object is given the opposite charge (or earthed) so droplets are attracted to it, even round the back.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: droplets repel → even spray; 1 mark: attracted to object → less waste.

(b) The rod is held near small pieces of paper. Explain why they jump to it. (c) Explain why the same experiment does not work with a metal rod held in the hand.
items.answer: (a) 1.0 × 10¹⁰ (b) Charge is induced on the paper: opposite charge near the rod, so attraction exceeds repulsion. (c) Charge flows through the conducting metal and the body to earth.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Why do metals conduct electricity? (b) Which material is an electrical conductor?
items.answer: (a) They contain free electrons that can move through the metal (b) Copper
items.markingKey: (a) Delocalised electrons carry charge. (b) Metals have free electrons that move through the lattice.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A rubbed balloon sticks to a neutral wall. Explain why. (b) Explain why charging by friction cannot produce a positive charge by "adding protons".
items.answer: (a) The negative balloon repels electrons in the wall surface away, leaving the surface positively charged by induction; unlike charges attract. (b) Protons are fixed in the nuclei; only electrons are free to move, so an object becomes positive by losing electrons.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: charge induced in wall; 1 mark: attraction of unlike charges. (b) 1 mark each.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the charge on a rubbed insulator stays in one place while charge on a conductor spreads out. (b) Explain how a metal sphere on an insulating stand can be charged by induction using a charged rod.
items.answer: (a) Electrons cannot move through an insulator, but in a conductor they move freely and repel each other, spreading over the surface. (b) Bring the rod near (electrons repelled or attracted), earth the far side briefly, remove the earth, then the rod: the sphere keeps an opposite charge.

items.stem: Classify these materials as conductors or insulators and explain the difference in terms of electrons: dry wood, silver, paper, copper.
items.answer: Conductors: silver, copper; insulators: dry wood, paper. Conductors have free electrons; insulators do not.

items.stem: A acetate strip is rubbed with a cotton cloth and becomes positively charged with a charge of magnitude 9.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ C. Describe the electric field pattern around the rod tip if it acts like a point charge.
items.answer: Radial lines pointing outwards.

items.stem: Classify these materials as conductors or insulators and explain the difference in terms of electrons: steel, plastic, copper, silver.
items.answer: Conductors: steel, copper, silver; insulators: plastic. Conductors have free electrons; insulators do not.

items.stem: A perspex ruler is rubbed with a silk and becomes positively charged with a charge of magnitude 1.6 × 10⁻⁹ C. (a) State the charge on the cloth. (b) Calculate the number of electrons transferred (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C). (c) The rod is held near small pieces of paper. Explain why they jump to it.
items.answer: (a) −1.6 × 10⁻⁹ C (equal and opposite) (b) 1.0 × 10¹⁰ (c) Charge is induced on the paper: opposite charge near the rod, so attraction exceeds repulsion.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) The electric field lines around an isolated positive point charge (b) The direction of an electric field at a point is the direction of the force on
items.answer: (a) point radially outwards (b) a small positive charge placed there
items.markingKey: (a) Lines leave positive charges and enter negative ones. (b) Field direction = direction of force on a positive test charge.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Describe the electric field between two parallel plates, one positive and one negative. (b) Explain how an electrostatic paint sprayer gives an even coat and wastes less paint.
items.answer: (a) Uniform: parallel, equally spaced lines from the positive plate to the negative plate (curving slightly at the edges). (b) Paint droplets are given the same charge, so they repel and spread out; the object is given the opposite charge (or earthed) so droplets are attracted to it, even round the back.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: parallel equally spaced; 1 mark: + to −. (b) 1 mark: droplets repel → even spray; 1 mark: attracted to object → less waste.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why you sometimes get a small shock touching a metal door handle after walking on a nylon carpet. (b) Describe the electric field between two parallel plates, one positive and one negative.
items.answer: (a) Friction between shoes and carpet charges your body; when you touch the earthed metal handle, charge flows suddenly through you to earth. (b) Uniform: parallel, equally spaced lines from the positive plate to the negative plate (curving slightly at the edges).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each. (b) 1 mark: parallel equally spaced; 1 mark: + to −.

items.stem: Describe the electric field pattern for a positive charge near a negative charge, and state the direction of the force on a small positive charge placed in the field.
items.answer: Lines curve from the positive to the negative charge. Force on a small positive charge: along the field lines.
items.markingKey: 2 marks pattern with direction; 1 mark force direction.

items.stem: A acetate strip is rubbed with a cotton cloth and becomes positively charged with a charge of magnitude 4.8 × 10⁻⁹ C. (a) Explain, in terms of electrons, how the rod became charged. (b) Calculate the number of electrons transferred (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C).
items.answer: (a) Electrons moved off the acetate strip onto the cloth. (b) 3.0 × 10¹⁰
